title: The Oath Kept: Carthage to Libyssa
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Oath: Carthage of the Barcids

stops.name: Carthage, the Byrsa hill
stops.campa: In the year the Romans and Carthaginians grind against each other in Sicily, a son is born to Hamilcar of the house of Barca, the Thunderbolt. They name him Hannibal: the Grace of Baal. The city climbs the Byrsa in white terraces above its double harbor; the sign of Tanit stands on ten thousand stelae; Melqart of Tyre keeps the sea-gates. The child opens his eyes on a city at war, and the war will never once let go of him.
suggested_refs: Barcid silver shekel, head of Melqart with club, war elephant reverse
Sign of Tanit stelae, Carthage

stops.name: The Tophet of Salammbô, the altar of Baal Hammon
stops.campa: Hamilcar, about to sail for Iberia, sacrifices to Baal Hammon and Tanit for a fair crossing. The victim burns; the omens are good. His son, nine years old, comes to the altar and begs, with a boy's coaxing, to be taken along. Hamilcar takes the child by the right hand, leads him up to the fire, and bids him lay his palm upon the sacrifice and swear. Hannibal swears. The flame takes the words, and the words take the man: the whole war to come is lit here, at this altar, in this small burning hand.
stops.quote: I swear that I will never be a friend to the Romans.
stops.quote_source: The oath as Hannibal himself recounted it to King Antiochus, Polybius 3.11; Livy 21.1; Nepos, Hannibal 2
suggested_refs: Benjamin West, The Oath of Hannibal (1770)
Giovanni Battista Pittoni, Hannibal Swearing Enmity to Rome
Tophet urns and stelae of Salammbô

stops.name: The harbors of Carthage, sailing for Iberia
stops.campa: From the round war-harbor, the Cothon, whose hidden sheds hold two hundred keels, Hamilcar's fleet stands out to sea. The boy who swore rides at his father's side. Carthage has lost Sicily and Sardinia and paid the indemnity of a defeated city; Hamilcar sails to build a new empire out of Iberian silver with which to pay Rome, and one day to fight her. Hannibal watches the Byrsa sink under the horizon. He will not see it again for thirty-six years.
suggested_refs: Reconstruction of the circular Punic war-harbor (Cothon) of Carthage

stops.name: Gades, the temple of Melqart at the Pillars
stops.campa: Landfall at Gades, oldest daughter of Tyre in the west, on her island at the edge of the world. Hamilcar sacrifices in the temple of Melqart, where an undying fire burns before a god who has no image, and barefoot priests in linen serve the emptiness. Beyond the temple there is only Ocean. The boy stands between the bronze pillars and learns the shape of his house's faith: the god of Tyre walks with the Barcids, west of everything.
suggested_refs: Sancti Petri islet, traditional site of the Herakleion of Gades
Phoenician bronze votives of Sancti Petri

stops.name: Akra Leuke, the white citadel
stops.campa: Hamilcar founds his white fortress above the sea and the boy grows up inside an army. Hannibal learns Iberian and Greek, the sarissa and the javelin, hunger and watch-keeping. The portrait the canon paints is formed here: first into the fight, last out of it; sleeping on the bare ground in a soldier's cloak among the sentries; eating what the ranks eat; on horse or foot beyond all others. The camp is his school, his father the only master.
suggested_refs: Tossal de Manises excavations, Alicante
Livy's character-portrait of Hannibal (21.4)

stops.name: Helike, the death of Hamilcar
stops.campa: Besieging Helike in winter, Hamilcar is caught by a sudden host of Oretani and Vettones. He turns his own horse against the pursuit to draw it away from his sons, and rides into the swollen river, and the water takes him. The Thunderbolt is quenched saving Hannibal and Hasdrubal, who live because their father chose the flood. Hannibal is eighteen. The oath now has no keeper but himself.
suggested_refs: Diodorus's account of Hamilcar's last ride

stops.name: New Carthage: Qart Hadasht of Hasdrubal, master of horse
stops.campa: Hasdrubal the Handsome, his sister's husband, builds a second Carthage on the lagoon: one gate to the land, silver mines at its back, the finest harbor of Iberia. Hannibal, come of age, commands the cavalry. The canon says no officer matched him: boldest in danger, coolest inside it; no toil could weary the body nor break the spirit; heat and cold alike endured. The army begins to look at him the way it once looked at his father.
suggested_refs: Punic wall of Cartagena
Barcid shekels struck at New Carthage

stops.name: New Carthage, acclaimed general at twenty-six
stops.campa: A Celtic slave's knife takes Hasdrubal, and the army does not wait for Carthage: the soldiers carry Hannibal to the headquarters tent and hail him general with one shout. He is twenty-six. The old campaigners weep, for they say Hamilcar is given back to them young: the same fire in the face, the same set of the eye. Carthage confirms what the camp has already sworn. The boy of the altar now holds the sword of the west.
suggested_refs: Marble bust called Hannibal, found at Capua (Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Naples)

stops.name: Althaea, the Olcades broken
stops.campa: His first campaign as general: he falls on the Olcades of the upper country, storms Althaea their strongest town, and the rest submit before the season turns. Tribute and levies flow to New Carthage. The canon notes the method that will empty Italy of certainty: speed before rumor, terror before speed, and generosity the moment the sword is sheathed. He winters rich, paying the army in full and something over.
suggested_refs: Polybius's summary of the Iberian campaigns (3.13-14)

stops.name: Castulo, the marriage of Imilce
stops.campa: At Castulo of the silver country, chief city of the Oretani, Hannibal takes an Iberian bride: Imilce, daughter of the town's great house. The tradition, which the poets carry, gives her a Greek descent and a son she will carry back to Carthage when the war calls her husband away. The marriage binds the mining heart of Iberia to the Barcids by blood. Of all his bonds, this one the canon barely allows him; the war eats even his household out of the record.
suggested_refs: Silius Italicus, Punica 3, Imilce's farewell
Cástulo archaeological site, Linares

stops.name: Helmantica (Salamanca), the Vaccaei and the women of the town
stops.campa: He drives north across the plateau farther than any Carthaginian has marched and takes Helmantica of the Vaccaei. The town surrenders, then breaks faith; and its women, allowed to walk out unarmed, carry the men's swords beneath their cloaks and put them back in their husbands' hands beyond the gates: a treachery so brave that Hannibal, retaking them, gives the women their freedom and their praise. Arbucala falls next after a long siege. The plateau learns his name.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, On the Bravery of Women 10, the women of Salmantica

stops.name: The Tagus ford, the Carpetani drowned
stops.campa: Returning laden with spoil, he is caught by the gathered nations: Carpetani with the fugitives of the Olcades and Vaccaei, a hundred thousand as the canon counts them. He refuses battle, slips across the Tagus by night, and stakes the far bank. When the host wades in, his horsemen ride them down in the stream and forty elephants trample the shallows; then he recrosses and breaks what remains. The river runs bodies. After the Tagus, no people south of the Ebro dares the field against him.
suggested_refs: Battle of the Tagus reconstructions

stops.name: Saguntum, the siege begins
stops.campa: Saguntum sits on its long rock above the sea, friend of Rome south of the Ebro: the tripwire both cities have laid and both pretend not to see. Hannibal invests it in the spring. The Saguntines hurl the falarica, the great fire-javelin with its burning tow, and fight like a city that expects the world to come save it. Under the wall a javelin passes through Hannibal's thigh; the siege slackens while he lies bleeding, then closes again harder. Rome sends envoys; he does not receive them. The world does not come.
suggested_refs: Castle ridge of Sagunto
The falarica of Saguntum (Livy 21.8)

stops.name: Saguntum, the fall in the eighth month
stops.campa: In the eighth month the towers come down and the town is taken street by street. The leading men heap their gold and silver into a fire in the forum and throw themselves after it; the rest die armed or under the roofs. The plunder pays an army and buys half of Carthage's council. Across the sea a Roman, Fabius, will soon stand in that council holding two folds of his toga, peace here, war here, and Carthage will answer: give us whichever you please. The fold falls open. It is war.
suggested_refs: Francisco Domingo Marqués, The Last Day of Sagunto (1869)
Fabius and the fold of the toga (Livy 21.18)

segments.name: The Great March: from the Pillars to the Alps

stops.name: Gades, the vows paid to Melqart
stops.campa: Before the great war he goes down to Gades, to the temple at the world's edge where he stood as a boy, and discharges his old vows to Melqart and binds himself with new ones. The god of his fathers, the wandering Herakles of Tyre, is made patron of the march: as Melqart once drove the cattle of the sun through these same lands to Italy, so the army will walk the god's own road. He returns to New Carthage with the god at his shoulder.
suggested_refs: Livy 21.21, the vows at Gades
The Heraklean Way, the god's road from the Pillars to Italy

stops.name: New Carthage, the muster of the nations
stops.campa: Spring opens the roads and the army stands on the parade grounds of Qart Hadasht: ninety thousand foot, twelve thousand horse, thirty-seven elephants, Libyans, Iberians, Numidians, slingers of the Balearics. He sends Iberian troops home to Africa and African troops to Iberia, each a hostage for the other's country; leaves his brother Hasdrubal the sea and the province; dismisses the doubtful to their villages with thanks, keeping only the willing. Then the trumpets, and the column uncoils toward the Ebro, and nothing about the world will be the same.
suggested_refs: Polybius 3.33, the muster figures from the Lacinian bronze

stops.name: The Ebro crossing, the dream of the serpent
stops.campa: The army crosses the Ebro in three columns, and that night the gods come for their general. In his sleep a youth of more than mortal beauty says he is sent by Jupiter to guide him into Italy: follow, and do not look back. Hannibal follows; then, as men must, he looks. Behind him a serpent of monstrous bulk drags itself forward, and forests and hillsides crash down before it, and a storm-cloud walks behind with thunder. What is this? he asks. The devastation of Italy, the youth answers. Go forward, and ask nothing more.
suggested_refs: Jan Miel, Il Sonno di Annibale
Cicero, De Divinatione 1.49, the dream from Coelius Antipater and Silenus

stops.name: The Pyrenees, the Col de Pertús
stops.campa: The tribes between Ebro and mountains are broken in weeks and Hanno is left to hold the new country. At the passes three thousand Carpetani, frightened less by the enemy than by the length of the road, turn for home; Hannibal, reading the army's heart, sends seven thousand more after them with his blessing, as if he had dismissed them himself. Fifty thousand foot and nine thousand horse, willing, all of them, cross the Pyrenees light. Fear stays behind on the Spanish side.
suggested_refs: Col du Perthus / Coll de Pertús, the traditional crossing

stops.name: Ruscino, the parley with the Gauls
stops.campa: The Gallic chiefs gather in arms at Ruscino, minded to bar the road. Hannibal invites them into his own camp instead: come to me, or I will come to you, and receives them with gifts and gold and the plain statement that he is a guest in Gaul, not an enemy, and will not draw a sword north of the mountains unless one is drawn on him. The chiefs go home rich and persuaded. The army passes through their country buying its bread, a wonder the Gauls speak of for a generation.
suggested_refs: Château-Roussillon (ancient Ruscino), Perpignan

stops.name: The Rhone, the elephants on the rafts
stops.campa: The Volcae mass on the far bank; Hanno son of Bomilcar swims a division across upstream on skins and fires their camp at the signal-smoke, and the crossing is won. Then the elephants: great piers of lashed rafts are run out from the bank, floored with earth so the beasts believe they walk on land; the females lead; when the towed sections swing into the current the elephants panic, and some plunge in and drown their mahouts, but the beasts themselves, trunks raised above the water, walk the riverbed and come up on the Italian side. The river is beaten. Scipio's scouts arrive to find only cold fires.
suggested_refs: Henri Motte, Hannibal Crossing the Rhone (1878)
Polybius 3.46, the elephants walking the riverbed

stops.name: The Island, the kingmaker at the Isère
stops.campa: Four days up the Rhone lies the Island, rich land in the fork of the rivers, where two brothers are at war for the kingship of the Allobroges. Hannibal, arriving with an army, is asked to judge between them, and crowns the elder, Brancus. The new king pays for his crown royally: grain, new boots for the whole army, wool cloaks against the mountains, weapons reissued, and an escort of his warriors to cover the rear. The Carthaginian walks toward the Alps shod and clothed by a king he made in an afternoon.
suggested_refs: Polybius 3.49, Brancus and the Island

stops.name: The Gates of the Alps, the first ambush
stops.campa: Where the escort turns back, the mountain Allobroges take up the tolls. They hold the heights above the one track, but only by day, going home to their town at dusk; Hannibal learns it from his Gallic scouts, lights his campfires as if bedded down, and takes the abandoned heights in the dark. At dawn the tribesmen attack anyway, and the column pays: horses hit by javelins scream and fall outward off the track, dragging their loads into the gorge. Hannibal comes down from his crag like a landslide himself, sweeps the attackers off, storms their white-walled town, and feeds the army three days from its stores.
suggested_refs: Heinrich Leutemann, Hannibals Übergang über die Alpen

stops.name: The White Rock, the second treachery
stops.campa: Higher up, elders come with branches and wreaths, offering guides and hostages. Hannibal trusts them exactly as far as their gorge: he puts the baggage and cavalry ahead and marches the heavy foot as rearguard, and when the guides spring the trap, boulders thundering down the couloirs, tribesmen on the slopes, the army is cut in two but not opened. All night Hannibal holds the bare white rock, the leukopetra the canon remembers, with half his force, apart from his horses and his baggage, until the column can reknit below. The mountains have now done their worst with men. What remains is the mountain itself.
suggested_refs: Polybius 3.52-53, the fight at the white rock

stops.name: The summit of the pass, the snows and the sight of Italy
stops.campa: On the ninth day the army stands on the roof of the world as the Pleiades set: new snow falling on old, the dead of the climb behind them, the beasts gaunt. Two days he rests them on the summit. Which summit, Clapier or Traversette, the canon itself has argued ever since. Then he gathers the men on the lip of the pass and shows them, far below and blue with distance, the plains of the Po: Italy, laid open like a taken city. Eighteen centuries on, a German poet will slip over these mountains southward, hungry for that same light. Hannibal enters it with elephants.
stops.quote: You are climbing over the walls not of Italy only, but of Rome herself. The rest of the road is smooth and downhill; one battle, or at most two, will put the citadel and capital of Italy into your hands.
stops.quote_source: Livy 21.35, the speech on the summit
suggested_refs: J. M. W. Turner, Snow Storm: Hannibal and his Army Crossing the Alps (1812)
Col de Clapier and Col de la Traversette, the debated passes

stops.name: The broken path, vinegar and fire
stops.campa: The descent is worse than the climb: the track falls away where a landslide has carried the mountainside off, and the army stands stopped above a precipice of new snow over old ice. Hannibal sets them to build. They fell the great trees and raise a pyre against the living rock; when the stone is furnace-hot they pour their ration of sour wine into it, and the boulder splits with a crack like the mountain's own bone breaking. Iron finishes what fire began; hairpins are cut into the cliff; in one day there is a road for mules, in three for elephants. Livy carries the story; the register carries Livy.
suggested_refs: Livy 21.37, infuso aceto, the vinegar in the rock
Nicolas Poussin, Hannibal Crossing the Alps on an Elephant

stops.name: The plains of the Taurini, the counting of the remnant
stops.campa: Fifteen days in the Alps; five months from New Carthage. On the grass of the Po valley he counts what the mountains have left him: twenty thousand foot, six thousand horse: the army halved, the survivors more like ghosts than men, the horses skeletal. The numbers are not rumor: Hannibal himself will engrave them in bronze at the temple of Hera on Cape Lacinium, and Polybius will read them there with his own eyes. With this remnant he proposes to break the greatest power in the world. He lets them eat, and the flesh comes back onto man and horse, and the ghosts become an army.
suggested_refs: Francisco de Goya, Hannibal the Conqueror Viewing Italy from the Alps (1771)
The Lacinian bronze tablet (Polybius 3.33, 3.56)

segments.name: The Thunderbolt in Italy: Ticinus to Cannae

stops.name: Taurini (Turin), the first lesson
stops.campa: The Taurini, at war with his would-be Gallic allies, decline his friendship. Their chief town holds three days; then it is taken, and everyone who bore arms in it is killed. It is not rage but arithmetic: the terror runs down the Po faster than any rider, and the wavering Gauls begin to come in. Before the walls he had paraded his Alpine captives and made them fight in pairs for freedom and a horse, so the army could watch its own condition made flesh: conquer, or die; there is no road back over the mountains.
suggested_refs: Polybius 3.62, the duels of the captives

stops.name: The Ticinus: first blood, and the boy Scipio
stops.campa: On the plain west of the Ticinus the horse of Carthage meets the horse of Rome, consul against general, and the Numidians fold around the Roman wings like water. The consul Publius Scipio goes down wounded in the press, and is cut free by a boy of seventeen who spurs in alone where his escort will not follow: his son, Publius Cornelius Scipio, one day to be called Africanus. The war's end rides onto the field at the war's first hour, and saves the life that will engender Zama. Rome retreats behind the Po by night, breaking the bridge.
suggested_refs: The rescue of the consul (Polybius 10.3; Livy 21.46)

stops.name: The Trebia, the ambush at the solstice
stops.campa: Snow and sleet at the winter solstice. Before dawn his Numidians bait the consul Sempronius across the Trebia: the Romans breakfastless, breast-deep in water running with ice. Hannibal's men have eaten by their fires and oiled themselves like athletes. In the streambed where the plain looks flat and hides everything, his brother Mago crouches with a thousand foot and a thousand horse, picked man by man. When the lines lock, Mago rises out of the earth at the Roman back. Elephants, cold, Numidians, ambush: the army of Rome breaks. Afterward the rains kill nearly every elephant, and the general goes on without them.
suggested_refs: The Trebbia battlefield south of Piacenza
Mago's ambush (Polybius 3.71)

stops.name: Winter among the Gauls, the man of many wigs
stops.campa: He winters among allies he does not trust. The Gallic chiefs, tired of a war eating their own fields, are known to weigh his murder; so Hannibal has wigs made, and clothes to match each one, now a greybeard, now a man in his prime, now a young dandy, changing them so constantly that not only strangers but his own friends pass him in the camp lanes without knowing him. The assassins can find no fixed man to kill. All winter the deadliest soldier alive walks his own camp as a rumor.
suggested_refs: Polybius 3.78, the wigs

stops.name: The Apennine ridge, beaten back by the storm
stops.campa: He tries the Apennines too early, and the mountain answers with a tempest the canon says was worse than anything in the Alps: rain driven level into the faces of the men, then hail, wind that tears every tent from its pegs, cold that kills. For once Hannibal turns back. The army shelters in the plain; more elephants die: after this only one remains alive, the great beast called Surus, the Syrian. Even the register of wonders records plainly: the weather defeated him where Rome had not.
suggested_refs: Livy 21.58, the storm on the ridge

stops.name: The marshes of the Arno, the eye given to Italy
stops.campa: To appear where no army can be, he takes the army where no army should go: four days and three nights through the flooded Arno country without dry ground to sleep on. Men doze on the packs of dead mules heaped in the water; the Gauls, marching in the churned middle of the column, sicken and despair; the Spaniards and Africans walk through on the firm bottom the unspoiled front provides. Hannibal rides the last elephant, Surus, above the fever-water, but the marsh takes its toll of him too: ophthalmia burns through his right eye. He comes out of the water half-blind and entirely unannounced, between Flaminius and Rome.
suggested_refs: Surus, the last elephant (Pliny, NH 8.11; Cato's Origines)
The one-eyed general on the elephant (Juvenal 10.157-158)

stops.name: Faesulae and the burning of Etruria, the baiting of Flaminius
stops.campa: Past Faesulae he turns the army loose on the richest country in Italy and burns it methodically, in sight of the consul's camp: smoke as a letter addressed to Flaminius personally. The consul is proud, popular, impatient of advice; Hannibal has studied him the way he studies ground. Omens pile up around the Roman: the consul's horse throws him, a standard cannot be pulled from the earth. Flaminius orders it dug out and follows the smoke. The trap he is walking toward is a lake shore shaped like a noose.
suggested_refs: The omens of Flaminius (Livy 22.3)

stops.name: Lake Trasimene, the battle in the fog
stops.campa: Mist off the lake fills the defile, and inside it waits the whole Carthaginian army, laid along the heights overnight. Flaminius marches his column in unscouted, and the hills come down on it from three sides with the lake as the fourth. Three hours of killing, so absorbed that a great earthquake passes through the battlefield unfelt. Ducarius the Insubrian knows the consul's face and drives his lance home; fifteen thousand die; the lake margins run red. Hannibal searches for Flaminius's body to bury it with honor; it is never found. Nineteen centuries on, Goethe will skirt this shore southward, in love with the Italy Hannibal holds by the throat.
suggested_refs: The earthquake unfelt (Livy 22.5; Pliny NH 2.86)
Tuoro sul Trasimeno battlefield and the ustrina burial pits

stops.name: Spoletium, the gate that will be called Flight
stops.campa: He probes south from the lake and is thrown back bloodily from the gates of Spoletium, a single Latin colony holding like a knot in wood. Hannibal reads the repulse as a measurement: if one colony costs this much, what is the price of Rome? He turns east for the Adriatic instead. The town will name a gate Porta della Fuga, the Gate of Flight, and keep the name for two thousand years. Goethe will stand in Spoleto one October marveling at the aqueduct; the town he marvels at is the town that said no.
suggested_refs: Porta della Fuga, Spoleto
Goethe, Italian Journey, Spoleto, October 1786

stops.name: Picenum, the horses bathed in old wine
stops.campa: On the Adriatic coast, in country fat with grain and orchards, he rests the army and repairs it like a smith repairing tools. The men eat until the marsh-sickness leaves them. The horses, mangy and worn to rope, he orders bathed in old wine, a prescription the canon records exactly, and their coats come back glossy under the Punic grooms' hands. Here too he re-arms his Libyans with captured Roman weapons, so that Africa now marches in Rome's own iron. From this shore he sends word by sea to Carthage for the first time since Spain: a letter of victories.
suggested_refs: Polybius 3.87-88, the wine-bath cure and the re-armed Africans

stops.name: The Falernian fields, the oxen with fire on their horns
stops.campa: Fabius the Delayer will not fight; he hangs on the hills like weather and lets Italy do the bleeding. When Hannibal gluts the army on the Falernian plain, Fabius quietly locks the one pass out of it. At night Hannibal has fagots lashed to the horns of two thousand captured oxen and the herds driven up the ridges, lit. The pass-guards see an army of torches flowing along the heights, abandon the defile, and fight smoke and cattle in the dark; the real army walks out through the empty pass, plunder and all. Fabius, fearing night and trickery equally, keeps his men in camp and watches the impossible fires burn.
suggested_refs: The stratagem of the oxen (Polybius 3.93-94; Livy 22.16-17)

stops.name: Gerunium, the granary winter and the cloud on the mountains
stops.campa: He takes Gerunium with its granaries full and winters in a town used as a barn. Rome, impatient with delay, splits the command: Minucius the bold is raised equal to Fabius the slow, and Hannibal, delighted, the canon says, to have half his enemy foolish, feeds Minucius a small victory, then draws him onto ground stitched with five hundred hidden horse and five thousand foot. The ambush closes; the master of horse is dying in the open when Fabius brings his legions down like a wall and Hannibal, unwilling to buy the whole meal at that price, withdraws. Walking back he says the storm has broken at last.
stops.quote: That cloud that has long been sitting on the tops of the mountains has burst at last in rain and storm.
stops.quote_source: Livy 22.30; Plutarch, Fabius 12, Hannibal on Fabius after the rescue of Minucius
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Fabius Maximus

stops.name: Cannae, the second of August
stops.campa: On the plain of the Aufidius, eight legions, the largest army Rome has ever fielded, advance into a line bent forward like a drawn bow: Gauls and Spaniards at the bulge, African veterans at the tips. The bow bends backward as it is pushed; the Romans wedge into their own funeral; the Africans fold onto the flanks; Hasdrubal's horse closes the rear. The double envelopment shuts like a hand. Volturnus drives dust into fifty thousand dying faces; the consul Paullus refuses a horse and dies with his army. It is the ancient world's bloodiest single day, designed by the man who at dawn made his officers laugh.
stops.quote: One thing, Gisgo, is more astonishing than their numbers: in all that great host over there, there is not one man named Gisgo.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Fabius 15, to the officer Gisgo, awed by the Roman numbers, at dawn before Cannae
suggested_refs: The Cannae battlefield and memorial column, Barletta
John Trumbull, The Death of Paulus Aemilius at Cannae (1773)

stops.name: The field of Cannae, next dawn: Maharbal's rebuke and the rings
stops.campa: Morning shows what the hand closed on: the dead lying in ranks where the ranks stood, some Romans found with their heads buried in dug earth, having smothered themselves. From the equestrian dead the gold rings are harvested, measured, the tradition says, in bushels, and sent to pour out on the floor of the Carthaginian senate house. Maharbal of the horse begs to ride at once: in five days, he swears, you dine on the Capitol. Hannibal answers that he must have time to deliberate. Then Maharbal says the sentence that the canon has never stopped repeating, and that day's delay, men will say forever, saves Rome.
stops.quote: You know how to win a victory, Hannibal; you do not know how to use one. — And Hannibal: I commend your zeal, Maharbal, but I need time to weigh the plan.
stops.quote_source: Livy 22.51, Vincere scis, Hannibal; victoria uti nescis
suggested_refs: Sébastien Slodtz, Hannibal counting the rings of the Roman knights (Louvre)
The bushels of rings (Livy 23.12)

segments.name: The Long Italian Twilight: Capua to the Recall

stops.name: Capua, the soft winter
stops.campa: Capua, second city of Italy, opens her gates and her houses, and the army that slept in Alpine snow winters in feather beds. Baths, wine, perfume, sleep past dawn: the canon insists that the city accomplished what Cannae could not, and the Romans will say ever after that Capua was Hannibal's Cannae. The register records the tradition and notes what the tradition forgets: that this same softened army will fight undefeated in Italy for thirteen more years. But something does end at Capua: the war stops being a lightning bolt and becomes a long weather.
suggested_refs: Livy 23.18, the winter quarters at Capua
The amphitheatre and ruins of ancient Capua, Santa Maria Capua Vetere

stops.name: Nola, the wall of Marcellus
stops.campa: Three times he comes at Nola and three times Marcellus, the man Rome calls her sword, as Fabius is her shield, throws him back from the gates, once sallying into the Carthaginian line as it deploys. The repulses are small; their meaning is not. For the first time since the Trebia, Roman soldiers learn that Hannibal's army can be made to step backward. The canon marks Nola the way a physician marks the hour a fever breaks: not the cure, but the first cool morning.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Marcellus 11-12, the fights at Nola

stops.name: Tarentum, the city taken through the hunting gate
stops.campa: Philemenus of Tarentum loves boar-hunting, and the Roman gate-guards have grown used to his horn in the small hours and the game he shares. On the chosen night the horn sounds as always; the postern opens for the hunter, and Hannibal's Africans come through it behind a dead boar carried like a trophy. Ten thousand men enter a sleeping city on the habits of one sentry. The citadel on its spit of rock holds out, Roman and stubborn, commanding the harbor mouth; Hannibal hauls the Tarentine ships across the city streets on wagons and launches them outside the trap: a fleet portaged through a town.
suggested_refs: Polybius 8.24-34, the night of Philemenus
The ships hauled through the streets (Polybius 8.34; Livy 25.11)

stops.name: The walls of Rome, Hannibal ad portas
stops.campa: To pry the besiegers off Capua he marches on Rome itself, and the cry that will frighten Roman children for five centuries is heard in earnest: Hannibal ad portas. He camps on the Anio, rides two thousand horse under the Colline Gate, examining the walls like a buyer, and hurls a spear over them, the oath's iron touching Rome at last. Twice the armies form for battle; twice hailstorms break the sky and part them. Word comes that the ground under his camp has sold at auction, at full price; he laughs, auctions the Forum's bankers' shops in reply, and turns away. He never sees the walls again.
suggested_refs: Hannibal ad portas (Cicero, Philippics 1.5.11)
The spear over the wall (Pliny, NH 34.15 tradition)
The auction of the ground (Livy 26.11)

stops.name: The hill near Venusia, the death of Marcellus
stops.campa: Marcellus, five times consul, the sword of Rome, rides out with a small party to scout a wooded hill between the camps. Numidians are lying in the trees. The sword of Rome dies in a skirmish no poet would have written for him. Hannibal comes to the body and stands over the man who beat him at Nola, takes the signet ring for war's uses, but will not take the corpse: he shrouds it, burns it with honor, and sends the ashes to the son in a silver urn. Even the canon of his enemies keeps this: no Roman ever mourned Marcellus more correctly than Hannibal did.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Marcellus 29-30, the funeral given by Hannibal

stops.name: Canusium, the head of Hasdrubal
stops.campa: Hasdrubal has done it: crossed the same Alps in half the time and marches down Italy to join hands with him. The letter naming the meeting-place is taken on the road, and the consul Nero force-marches north in secret, joins his colleague, and destroys Hasdrubal on the Metaurus. Hannibal, waiting in Apulia for word, receives it: Nero's horsemen fling a head before the Carthaginian outposts. Hannibal has it brought to him and looks a long time at the face of the brother who swore no oath and kept his anyway. Then he says the sentence, and draws the army back into Bruttium, into the toe of Italy.
stops.quote: Now I recognize the fortune of Carthage.
stops.quote_source: Livy 27.51, agnoscere se fortunam Carthaginis, on seeing Hasdrubal's head
suggested_refs: The Metaurus battlefield tradition, Marche
Livy 27.51

stops.name: Cape Lacinium, the bronze tablet in Hera's temple
stops.campa: At the temple of Hera Lacinia, Hannibal dedicates an altar and a great bronze tablet engraved in Punic and Greek: his own account of his marches and musters, set down in the goddess's keeping. Polybius will stand here, copy the figures, and trust bronze over rumor. The temple holds a column of solid gold; the tradition says Hannibal bored it to test it and meant to take it, and the goddess warned him in a dream that she would take his one good eye, so he left the column and crowned it with a golden heifer cast from the borings. Even the wonders obey him only halfway.
suggested_refs: The Lacinian tablet (Polybius 3.33, 3.56; Livy 28.46)
The golden column and the dream of Juno (Cicero, De Divinatione 1.24.48)
Capo Colonna, Crotone

stops.name: Croton, the recall to Africa
stops.campa: Scipio is in Africa, and the senate of Carthage sends the order no Roman army could compel: come home. Fifteen years in Italy, undefeated in the field, and it ends with an instruction on a ship. The canon says he gnashed his teeth and could scarcely keep from tears; that he raged at the men, not Rome, who starved him of reinforcement; that he cursed himself for not marching on Rome with his sword bloody. The grim tradition adds that Italian soldiers refusing the crossing were killed in the goddess's precinct. He looks back at Italy as few exiles ever looked back at their own country. Then Africa.
suggested_refs: Livy 30.20, the leaving of Italy
The Bruttium coast at Crotone

stops.name: Hadrumetum, landfall after thirty-six years
stops.campa: The fleet raises the African coast and he steps ashore at Hadrumetum, south of Carthage: a boy of nine when he left this country, a one-eyed man of forty-four returning with the wreck of an empire to save. He does not go up to Carthage; he builds an army instead, folding his Italian veterans, the men of Cannae, grey now, around new levies and Numidian horse bought with whatever Numidia will still sell. Rome's war has come home to the land where the oath was sworn.
suggested_refs: Sousse (ancient Hadrumetum), the Punic harbor town

stops.name: The plain of Naraggara, the parley of the two captains
stops.campa: Between the two camps, on ground Scipio has chosen and Hannibal has accepted, the two greatest soldiers of the age ride out, one interpreter apiece, and meet for the first time. For a moment, Polybius says, they look at each other in silence, in wonder. Hannibal speaks first: the elder, the invader, the man who has seen fortune from both sides. He offers peace and speaks of chance; Scipio answers that the time for terms was before he crossed to Africa. They part with courtesy and no agreement, each knowing the other told the truth. Tomorrow the world will be decided by professionals who respect each other completely.
stops.quote: The best fortune would have been that Rome had never desired anything beyond Italy, nor Carthage beyond Africa. A certain peace is better and safer than a hoped-for victory: the one is in your own power, the other in the hands of the gods.
stops.quote_source: Livy 30.30; Polybius 15.6-7, Hannibal to Scipio at the parley before Zama
suggested_refs: The parley of Hannibal and Scipio (Livy 30.30; Polybius 15.6-8)

stops.name: Zama, the last field
stops.campa: Eighty elephants open the battle, and Scipio opens lanes and blows them through with trumpets. Massinissa's Numidians, Hannibal's own weapon his whole life, ride this day for Rome and strip the Carthaginian flanks. Line by line the army is spent until only the third stands: the veterans of Italy, held back for the end, fighting to a standstill until the Roman cavalry returns at their backs: Cannae inverted, executed on its inventor. Twenty thousand fall. Hannibal cuts his way out and rides for Hadrumetum, having done, Polybius judges, everything a great general could do. The field itself the canon never fixes; the register holds the tradition.
suggested_refs: Cornelis Cort after Giulio Romano, The Battle of Zama (engraving)
Henri-Paul Motte, The Battle of Zama

stops.name: Carthage, the tears and the laughter
stops.campa: He enters Carthage after thirty-six years as the advocate of surrender. When Gisgo rises in the assembly to argue against the peace, Hannibal, a soldier ignorant, he admits, of city manners, drags him from the rostrum, then apologizes: he left this city at nine; let them pardon a man who grew up in a camp. When the terms are read and the senators weep, he laughs aloud, and answers their fury like a surgeon: the time for weeping was when the arms were surrendered and the ships burned; they cry now because the wound has reached their purses. Carthage takes the peace, and takes the man.
stops.quote: If one could see the state's inward mind as one sees a face, this laughter would not seem to you the laughter of joy but of a heart half-mad with its miseries. The time for your tears was when our arms were taken from us and our ships were burned; you weep now because the loss touches your own purses.
stops.quote_source: Livy 30.44 (condensed), Hannibal to the weeping senate of Carthage
suggested_refs: Livy 30.37, 30.44, the rostrum and the laughter

stops.name: Byrsa, the suffete against the Hundred and Four
stops.campa: Carthage elects the beaten general suffete, and the oligarchs learn that the breaker of armies breaks account-books too. He audits the state and finds the Roman tribute stolen twice over by its collectors; and when the Hundred and Four, life-tenured judges, the shadow senate that crucifies generals, shield the thieves, he carries a law before the people making the judges elected year by year, none twice running. In one summer he unmakes the oligarchy and pays the indemnity from recovered graft, no new tax. The Hundred and Four do what Rome could not: they write to the senate that Hannibal plots with Antiochus, and the commissioners sail.
suggested_refs: Livy 33.45-47, the suffete's reform
The Byrsa quarter, Carthage

segments.name: The Exile: from Tyre to Libyssa

stops.name: The tower by the sea, between Acylla and Thapsus
stops.campa: The Roman commissioners land pretending other business, and Hannibal does not wait for the pretense to ripen. He shows himself in the forum until evening, then rides out of Carthage in the dark with two companions, changing horses through the night, and by morning is at his own tower on the coast between Acylla and Thapsus, where, because he has expected exile for years, a ship lies provisioned with a crew that asks nothing. The greatest citizen Carthage ever produced leaves her forever between a sunset and a sunrise, a fugitive from his own countrymen more than from Rome.
suggested_refs: Livy 33.47-48, the night ride to the coast

stops.name: Cercina, the tent of sails
stops.campa: At Cercina the harbor is full of Phoenician merchantmen, any one of which could carry word to Carthage before him. Recognized at once, he announces he is an envoy bound for Tyre, and invites every shipmaster to a feast on the beach; and since it is midsummer, might they not lend their sails and yards for shade? The awning goes up, made of every sail in the harbor; the wine goes late. In the first dark of morning his ship slips out alone. The masters wake at noon under their own borrowed canvas, hours of rigging from any pursuit. He has escaped an island with a dinner party.
suggested_refs: Livy 33.48, the banquet of the sails
Kerkennah Islands

stops.name: Tyre, the mother city
stops.campa: He sails east along the whole spine of the sea to Tyre, the mother of Carthage, and the founders' city receives the exile as a son of the house come home: the canon says he was welcomed with every honor, as if born there. In the temple of Melqart of Tyre, the original fire of which Gades and Carthage burn copies, the circle closes on itself: Dido sailed west from this rock to found the city that raised him; her city has cast him out; the first city takes him back. He rests, and the east begins to learn what the west could not hold.
suggested_refs: Livy 33.49, the welcome at Tyre
The temple of Melqart at Tyre (Herodotus 2.44)

stops.name: Ephesus: the court of Antiochus, and the oath retold
stops.campa: At Ephesus he joins Antiochus the Great, the one king with weight enough to be Rome's counterpoise, and the king acquires both a weapon and a problem: Roman envoys make a show of long friendly visits to Hannibal, and the poison works: Antiochus cools. So Hannibal tells the king the one story that cannot be doubted: the altar at Carthage, his father's hand, the oath of a nine-year-old kept for fifty years. Antiochus hears it and believes, and the suspicion dies. Later, reviewing his gilded, jewel-crusted army, the king asks whether all this will be enough for the Romans, and receives the canon's most expensive joke.
stops.quote: Yes, quite enough for the Romans, I think — even though they are the greediest men alive.
stops.quote_source: Aulus Gellius 5.5, Hannibal to Antiochus reviewing the gilded army; the oath retold: Polybius 3.11
suggested_refs: Polybius 3.11, the oath told at Ephesus
Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 5.5

stops.name: Ephesus, the second meeting with Scipio
stops.campa: Scipio Africanus comes east with an embassy, and the two old enemies meet again: no armies now, two middle-aged men walking and talking. Who was the greatest general? Alexander, says Hannibal: with a small army he routed innumerable hosts and reached the world's ends. Second? Pyrrhus: no man ever chose ground better. Third? Myself. Scipio laughs: and if you had beaten me? The answer is the most perfect courtesy ever paid inside a boast; the canon of three nations keeps it. That season, after the philosopher Phormio lectures him on war for hours, Hannibal remarks he has seen many old madmen: none madder than Phormio.
stops.quote: Then, had I beaten you, I should have placed myself before Alexander, before Pyrrhus, before all.
stops.quote_source: Livy 35.14; Plutarch, Flamininus 21; Appian, Syriaca 10, the generals exchange. Phormio: Cicero, De Oratore 2.75
suggested_refs: Hannibal and Scipio at Ephesus (Livy 35.14)
The library quarter of Ephesus

stops.name: Off Side, the sea-fight at the Eurymedon
stops.campa: Antiochus, taking none of his plan to carry the war to Italy itself as Hannibal had urged, gives him instead a fleet, the one weapon he has never wielded. Off Side, near the mouth of the Eurymedon, Hannibal commands at sea for the only time in his life, against the Rhodians, the finest sailors afloat. His own wing presses theirs and breaks ships; the Rhodian center and left shatter the Seleucid line, and the day is lost. It is the single defeat of his career before Zama's shadow-country, and the register records it without flinching: the god of Tyre gave him the land, and the sea he gave to Rhodes.
suggested_refs: Livy 37.23-24, the battle of Side

stops.name: Gortyn, Crete: the gold in the statues
stops.campa: After Magnesia breaks Antiochus, the peace names Hannibal for surrender, and he vanishes to Gortyn on Crete. He arrives rich, and Cretans notice riches. So he fills amphorae with lead, crusts the tops with gold and silver, and deposits them in Diana's temple with grave ceremony, before witnesses, entrusting his fortune to Gortynian honor. The town posts a guard on the temple: watching, above all, Hannibal. His actual gold he pours into battered bronze statues tumbled like junk in his courtyard. When he sails he carries his trash and leaves the Cretans faithfully guarding his lead. The old lion, the canon smiles, out-foxes a whole island.
suggested_refs: Nepos, Hannibal 9, the amphorae of lead
The ruins of Gortyn

stops.name: Artaxata, the Armenian Carthage
stops.campa: The trail bends inland, to the court of Artaxias of Armenia, and here the destroyer becomes a founder. He sees an elbow of land in the Araxes, river-ringed but for a narrow isthmus, Ararat on the horizon like a witness, ground read by the same eye that read Cannae, and he persuades the king to set his capital there, and lays out the city himself. Artaxata rises on Hannibal's plan and is called the Armenian Carthage: the city of a man whose own city cast him out, planted at the earth's far end from Rome. Plutarch carries it, Strabo carries it, and the register builds the walls.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Lucullus 31, Hannibal the architect of Artaxata
Khor Virap and the Araxes plain below Ararat

stops.name: Prusa, the court of Bithynia
stops.campa: The last court that will have him is the smallest: Prusias of Bithynia, a cautious king in a poor kingdom at war with Eumenes of Pergamon, Rome's favorite. Hannibal, near seventy, pays for his shelter in the only coin he has ever carried: victories. He directs the king's war, and in the quiet between campaigns founds a city for him at the foot of the Mysian Olympus: Prusa, which will live under that mountain for two thousand years. Two cities standing at opposite ends of the world, Artaxata and Prusa, are the exile's monuments: the man who could not save his own city kept building other people's.
suggested_refs: Pliny, NH 5.43, Prusa founded by Hannibal
Bursa beneath Uludağ (the Mysian Olympus)

stops.name: The Propontis, the serpent-pots of the Bithynian fleet
stops.campa: Outnumbered at sea by Pergamon, Hannibal fights his last battle with pottery. He has the country scoured for venomous snakes, sealed by the thousand into clay jars; then, to find the king among his ships, sends a herald with a letter under the caduceus: the letter is mere insult; its course marks the royal flagship. The order: every Bithynian ship converges on Eumenes alone; against the rest, the jars. The pots arc over the water and burst on the Pergamene decks; the sailors laugh, until the decks begin to move. Pergamon's fleet flees a rain of snakes, and the old man takes his last victory from the earth.
suggested_refs: Nepos, Hannibal 10-11, the serpent-pots
The herald and the letter marking the flagship

stops.name: Libyssa, the house of seven doors and the ring
stops.campa: Flamininus comes to Bithynia, and the cautious king weighs an old guest against Rome and chooses Rome. Soldiers close on the house at Libyssa. Hannibal, who has expected every betrayal since the first, built it with seven doors, but a runner from each returns with the same word: soldiers, at all of them. He calls for the poison carried for years beneath the stone of his ring, kept for this one unwatchable door; curses Prusias, calling hospitality's gods to witness the broken faith; speaks the last sentence, level as a ledger; and drinks. He is sixty-four. That same season Scipio dies in his own exile at Liternum.
stops.quote: Let us relieve the Roman people of their long anxiety, since they think it long to wait for the death of an old man.
stops.quote_source: Livy 39.51, liberemus diuturna cura populum Romanum
suggested_refs: Livy 39.51; Nepos, Hannibal 12; Plutarch, Flamininus 20, the death at Libyssa
The poison ring

stops.name: The tumulus of Libyssa, the grave
stops.campa: They bury him where he fell, in a mound above the Gulf of Nicomedia, and Libyssa fades until, in Pliny's day, it is remembered for one thing: the tumulus of Hannibal. Tradition says Septimius Severus, the African-born emperor, faced the mound in white marble four centuries on. The exact spot slips from human knowledge, the canon's last honest gap, but travelers still seek it on the hillsides between Gebze and the water, where another soldier-founder of another republic ordered the grave honored again. The oath is discharged: nine years old at the altar, sixty-four at the ring, and never, not for one hour, a friend of Rome.
suggested_refs: Pliny, NH 5.43, Libyssa known for the tumulus
Tzetzes on Severus's marble facing
The Hannibal memorial at Gebze
